Where to sail this week

This analysis was written Monday 2 pm. The ratings, call and hour-by-hour tables have been auto-updated Thu 12:40 pm from newer forecasts; where they differ, trust the numbers.

The week's analysis

Monday, October 26, 2026, 2 pm · for Seattle-area windsurfers

Bottom line: one big desert day, but not worth a day off. Tuesday afternoon Temira has 25 to 28 mph westerlies from Rowena or Avery out to Threemile, ahead of Wednesday's colder front. That rates 5 stars at Maryhill, Roosevelt and Threemile, but it builds through the late morning and gives about 4 hours of planing for a 7.5 to 8 hour round trip, short of the bar. Our desert numbers also ran 4 to 5 mph high twice last week. Wednesday has 15 to 28 mph in the desert again with rain, then Thursday and Friday go light and offshore. Home water: SW 10 to 15 kt on the Sound Tuesday afternoon, the best local chance, in rain. If you can work from the RV, Maryhill to Threemile holds 3+ stars Monday to Wednesday.

How last week's forecast did

From Oct 19 to 25 the automatic grading checked 57 spot-days against NOAA stations and the Gorge airports: 48 came within one star (84%). The overall track record is now 146 of 186 verified spot-days within one star (79% weighted), with a typical speed error of about 4 mph.

  • Missed: home-water northerlies. West Point read N 12 to 13 kt on the afternoons of Oct 19, 20 and 22 while we had light wind or 6 to 10 mph: three decent Golden Gardens and Carkeek afternoons we under-called.
  • Too high: the Gorge on Oct 22 and 23. We had W 14 to 25 mph at Mosier and Maryhill; The Dalles airport averaged 11 to 13 kt, and on Friday it veered NW. The Westport northwesterly on Oct 22 was the reverse: 25 kt measured against our 21 to 25 mph.
  • Under: the Rooster Rock easterly on Oct 20 (Troutdale 16 kt against our 11 to 15 mph).

Calibration has already folded these in; keep the desert Gorge overshoot in mind for Tuesday.

Your week, day by day

Multi-day runs worth the RV

Afield

Desert Gorge, Tuesday: 15 to 18 mph early, 21 to 24 by late morning, 25 to 28 in the afternoon (Temira). That's small-sail weather; see the gear calculator for sizes. Air 60°F, Columbia 59.9°F: a 4/3 or 5/4 suit. Rufus Landing overnight parking ends Oct 31 and Maryhill sites 51 to 71 close the same day. Recheck Temira's Tuesday morning post before you leave: if rain and clouds hold the wind east of Avery, Maryhill sits on the edge.

Wednesday: early westerlies of 15 to 20 mph from Rooster Rock to Viento (a morning window), then 15 to 28 in the desert in the afternoon with rain and highs in the low 50s. Snow drops to 2,500 to 3,500 ft Tuesday night, so expect snow on the passes.

Wallula Gap shows SW 17 to 21 mph Wednesday in the NWS grid, but its good directions are only inferred from geography, so it is never recommended.

BC: Howe Sound turns to N outflow 25 to 35 kt Thursday, which is not the southerly thermal Squamish needs. Haro Strait has SW 10 to 20 kt near noon Tuesday for Victoria.

Weekend and Winduro

The Winduro season ends Oct 31. Offshore NE flow Thursday and Friday and a cool, drier weekend give no daytime southerly so far; the call is due Thursday. Temira sees no clear sign of 15+ mph Gorge wind after Friday.

Home water: cold and current

Cold: the Sound is in the low to mid 50s now and 45 to 48°F from November to March. Wear a 5/4 hooded suit with booties and gloves or a drysuit, and assume every swim lasts longer than you expect. Highs drop to the low 50s after Wednesday.

Currents: in the main basin the flood runs south and the ebb runs north. In Tuesday's southwesterly the flood runs with the wind (smoother water, but you drift north on the ebb), so check NOAA current predictions before you go.

Golden Gardens and Carkeek: last week the northerlies outran our forecast three times. On a gray afternoon with a N breeze, check West Point (WPOW1) at lunch.

Self-rescue: sail with your buddy, carry a phone in a waterproof pouch, tell someone your plan, and practice controlled drifting before you need it. Call 911 for Seattle Harbor Patrol or the Coast Guard.

      How the stars are calculated

      Stars come from the forecast wind numbers only, with the same rules for every spot and day.

      1. Input. The sustained wind range forecast for that spot and day, in mph. NWS and Environment Canada forecasts are in knots and were converted (1 kt is 1.15 mph). Temira's Gorge forecast is already in mph. Gusts are shown but not counted.
      2. Speed band. Take the midpoint of the range. Under 8 mph is 0 stars, 8 to 11 is 1, 11 to 14 is 2, 14 to 18 is 3, 18 to 23 is 4, 23 to 28 is 5. The same bands drive the "what to bring" kit table: foil or longboard below 14, the 125 L board from 18 up. Sustained 28 mph or more is overpowered and is capped at 4.
      3. Timing penalty. A window of about 2 hours or less (after 5 pm, or evening only) subtracts 3 stars, because rigging and launching use up most of it. A window of 3 to 4 hours (morning only, or dawn to mid-morning) subtracts 1. Afternoon, all-day or split windows subtract nothing.
      4. Confidence penalty. Subtract 1 star when the source itself states low confidence. This week that is NWS Pendleton's roughly 30% confidence in Monday's Cascade gap-wind speeds (Vantage, Desert Aire, Lake Wenatchee, Rimrock, Lake Cle Elum).
      5. Direction cap. The forecast direction must be within 45° of a good direction listed for that spot (from nw-windtalk and the spot guides). If it is 45° or more away, the spot is capped at 1 star. Spots with no documented direction skip this step.
      6. Floor and gaps. Stars never go below 0. Days beyond a forecast's range (British Columbia Wednesday and Thursday) show a dash, not a guess.
      7. Distance bands. Spots are grouped by drive time from north Seattle: under 30 minutes, 30 minutes to 2½ hours, 2½ to 4 hours, and over 4 hours. A band's stars for a day equal its best spot that day. Ties go to the spot with the right wind direction, then to a sourced rather than estimated forecast, then to the shorter drive. "Browse by area" groups the same ratings by region instead.

      Discipline fit and gear. A spot-day "fits" a discipline from the same midpoint wind, as long as the direction is not capped and the window is not under 2 hours: longboard from 6 to 14 mph, foil from 8 to 18 mph, planing from 14 mph up. These come from windtalk reports (City League longboards racing in 3 to 18 mph, first foil flights in 8 to 10 kt, smooth foil flights at 13 to 17 mph, fin boards planing from the mid teens) and your gear's limits. Gear picks come from the "Your quiver" table at your weight.

      Not included: water temperature, tides, currents, swell, launch quality, crowds and the drive itself.

      Where the numbers come from: each spot's wind range comes from the forecast named in its "Basis" line: NWS marine forecasts and forecast discussions, Environment Canada marine forecasts, or Temira's Gorge forecast. Turning a zone forecast into one spot's local wind took judgment, and speeds marked "estimate" (Roads End) are my own inference from coast-wide forecasts. All the inputs, the formula and the results are saved with source ids in the database that goes with this page.

      One scale everywhere. The Spots grid, this dashboard and the analysis all use these stars. My earlier 0 to 4 judgment ratings are kept in the database for comparison; for this forecast they agree with the stars within one step on 319 of the 320 spot-days that have a forecast.

      Your quiver: what to bring

      Sized for your boards and your 10 to 3.7 m sails. Tap any day on the grid to see the pick for that spot and forecast. Set your weight in the box below. Fin-board sails shift about 1 m2 per 22 lb (a sail maker's rule of thumb), foil sails about half that; the bands come from windtalk session reports, including a 190 lb sailor fully powered on a 4.7 at 26 mph average.

      Pick a day

      Tap a day to highlight it in the grid. A warm ridge holds all week. The Gorge is the busy place: east wind Sunday morning, a solid westerly Monday that eases through Wednesday, then east wind again Thursday. Monday also brings gap winds to Vantage and a westerly to the Strait.

      Colors and the small number show stars, the same 0 to 5 scale as the dashboard. Arrows point the way the wind blows. Speeds are the expected afternoon range in mph. Tap a spot name for its full profile, starting with what nw-windtalk members say, or a square for that day's wind.

      Reading the Gorge sensors

      From Temira at The Gorge Is My Gym: the sensors don't agree, so translate before you rig.

      30 at Rufusis about 23 to 24 at Swell
      30 at Swellis about 35 to 37 at Rufus, Viento or Arlington
      25 at Swellis about 31 to 32 at Arlington
      38+ at Arlingtonmeans giant, glassy swell
      • The Hatch fires when Portland is cloudy and Hood River is sunny. A clear Portland sky often means an afternoon die-off, so head east to Lyle, Rowena or Doug's.
      • Arlington fires when it is cloudy, rainy and cool west of The Dalles, mostly in spring and fall.
      • Rufus loses its swell above about 325,000 cfs of river flow; check John Day Dam.
      • Water right now: Columbia about 66°F, Puget Sound and the coast about 58°F, the Strait about 51°F.
      • Passes: Discover Pass ($45 a year or about $10 to $11.50 a day) for the Hatch, Doug's and Maryhill; Oregon State Parks for Rooster Rock, Viento and Rowena; $80 CGW2 pass for Swell City; Port of Hood River pass or hourly parking on the waterfront.
